character_and_relationship_context: Aminata Diallo lives in a rented room on the outskirts of Bamako with no running water; she carries water from a communal stand. She works as the only woman and youngest on a construction crew, trained by master mason Sékou for two years. Sékou calls her "la petite comptable" because she recalculates load-bearing estimates in her head. He trusts her numbers and treats her like a protégée but never offers favors. The site manager barely knows her name and only sees her as a reliable extra hand. Aminata's mother died when she was twelve after a miscalculated loan caused her to lose her market stall. Since then, Aminata counts everything: bricks, costs, weeks until her accounting exam. She keeps a notebook of figures and dates, and hides an emergency fund under a floorboard, never touched. She studies at night by kerosene lamp after ten hours of hauling cement. She is saving for an accounting course and for a proper room for her sister, but does not speak of it. She routinely stays late to double-check measurements without pay, has never asked for an advance on her wage, and when faced with unexpected requests, she first calculates the cost in time before answering.
objective_situation: At the end of the day, as the crew packs up, Sékou walks over to Aminata. The site manager needs someone to stay an extra hour tonight to do the weekly inventory count before the next delivery arrives in the morning. The manager is about to leave, so Sékou says, 'Decide now, little comptable. Do you take it?' There is no overtime pay, only the responsibility. Aminata has her accounting notebook waiting at home and a long walk back. She has to answer before Sékou turns to leave.
state_and_available_memories: Aminata is physically exhausted after ten hours of hauling cement, her eyes burn from dust, and she has a two-hour walk ahead if she leaves now. Her accounting notebook is at home, and tonight's study session is already shortened. Immediate memories: The phrase 'weekly count' pulls her back to the last inventory, where she was the only one who noticed the cement bags on the delivery sheet didn't match the pile. The site manager's hurried tone reminds her of the time her mother's loan was called in without warning.
name: Aminata Diallo
